summary: A first-person account by Lieutenant Michael Jennings of the city's Fire and Emergency Services describing the multi-agency response to a massive power outage that began on September 15, 2023, in a city of over a million people. It traces the response from the initial call through stabilization by late September and into October reflection and planning. The account stresses inter-agency collaboration, community-led innovation, the human toll, and lessons learned to strengthen future emergency management.
one_line: Lieutenant Michael Jennings reflects on the multi-agency response and recovery after the September 15, 2023 citywide power outage and the lessons learned.
key_facts: A massive power outage struck the city on the morning of September 15, 2023, followed by internet and other utility failures.
The blackout stemmed from a critical failure in the city's aging infrastructure rather than a predictable disaster.
Lieutenant Michael Jennings of the city's Fire and Emergency Services answered the call at exactly 07:23 a.m.
The city is a metropolis of more than a million people; traffic lights went out during the morning rush and hospitals relied on generators.
Representatives from utilities, local government, police, fire, and emergency medical services convened at a hastily assembled Incident Command Center.
By September 22, the outage had caused a domino effect including small fires from malfunctioning generators, crimes of opportunity, and accidents in darkened streets.
Resource allocation and prioritization of recovery efforts were contentious issues among agencies.
By September 29, utility companies and emergency teams had restored power to a majority of affected areas, internet was patchy but returning, and public transport was on a provisional schedule.
Social media and digital platforms were used to provide updates and facilitate community assistance despite erratic connectivity.
Communities set up bicycle-powered charging stations, and cafes sheltered and fed emergency workers and displaced citizens.
Mental health professionals and community volunteers provided counseling and aid to those affected.
In the first week of October, agencies shifted to reflection and long-term planning, scheduling workshops and joint training sessions and analyzing incident data to build stronger reaction protocols.
